summary:
Orvyntex is an interactive web-based platform designed to support lunar mission planning, simulate lunar base operations, and educate users about the challenges of living beyond Earth.

Our project brings together astronomical calculations, mission scenario analysis, interactive operational simulations, and human spaceflight education into a single integrated experience.
details:
ORVYNTEX is organized into four interconnected modules that guide users through different stages of a lunar mission.

1. Lunar Landing Planner

The Lunar Landing Planner allows users to evaluate potential landing sites and mission dates by calculating the positions of the Sun and Earth relative to a selected location on the lunar surface.

Users can configure and compare up to five different mission scenarios, selecting predefined lunar sites or entering custom geographic coordinates and landing dates.

The application provides interactive astronomical visualizations, including a 360-degree local horizon view, a mission timeline, and a comparison of key environmental conditions.

Each scenario is evaluated using several indicators:

  • Sunlight: The percentage of the mission during which the Sun is visible above the modeled horizon.
  • Direct-to-Earth Contact: The percentage of the mission during which Earth is geometrically visible for direct communication.
  • Sun and Earth Together: The availability of simultaneous solar illumination and Earth visibility.
  • Longest Continuous Light: The longest uninterrupted period of solar illumination.
  • Maximum Solar Elevation: The highest angle reached by the Sun above the local horizon.
  • Viability Index: An integrated project-defined indicator that summarizes relevant mission conditions.

The platform also identifies continuous communication windows and allows users to explore how astronomical conditions change over time.

To strengthen scientific reliability, our astronomical calculations were compared against NASA's JPL Horizons system. Across 88 Sun and Earth position comparisons at four lunar sites for December 2026, the reported maximum angular difference was 0.014 degrees.

This allows users to explore how different locations and mission dates can significantly affect opportunities for solar power generation and direct communication with Earth.

2. Lunar Control Center

The Lunar Control Center extends mission planning into an interactive lunar base simulation.

Users can explore potential base locations, evaluate their environmental characteristics, establish infrastructure, and manage the challenges associated with maintaining a lunar settlement.

Through an interactive three-dimensional environment, the platform introduces concepts such as site exploration, resource management, energy availability, infrastructure development, and crew survival throughout a simulated 180-day mission.

The module also includes ORVY, an interactive assistant designed to guide users through the process of establishing and operating a lunar base.

This experience is inspired by the remote operations centers used in Chile's autonomous mining industry, where complex machinery and distributed operations are supervised from centralized control facilities.

While the Lunar Landing Planner uses astronomical calculations, the Lunar Control Center uses illustrative terrain and simulated operational conditions for educational purposes. This distinction allows the platform to combine scientific analysis with accessible experimentation without presenting simulated infrastructure or terrain as verified scientific data.

3. Living on the Moon

This educational module explores how the human body and everyday activities are affected by different gravitational environments.

Users can compare life on Earth, in orbital microgravity, and on the lunar surface, understanding how changes in gravity influence human physiology, movement, and daily routines.

The module includes eight interactive experiences covering:

  • Eating and drinking.
  • Sleeping and resting.
  • Walking and jumping.
  • Breathing and obtaining oxygen.
  • Cardiovascular function and fluid distribution.
  • Showering and personal hygiene.
  • Crying and tear behavior.
  • Orientation and balance.

Through visual demonstrations, interactive comparisons, and knowledge challenges, users can explore the scientific principles behind human spaceflight in an engaging and accessible format.

The objective is to help users understand that lunar exploration involves not only engineering and technology, but also the adaptation and well-being of the human body.

4. Mission Report

The Mission Report consolidates the results of the selected landing scenario and the lunar base simulation.

It presents astronomical indicators, mission viability assessments, communication and illumination opportunities, operational results, scientific methods, limitations, and the project's development roadmap.

For example, a simulated mission at the Shackleton–de Gerlache ridge beginning on December 1, 2026, produces 100% modeled solar illumination over a 14-day period but no direct visibility of Earth. Although the location offers favorable illumination conditions during this scenario, direct-to-Earth communication would require reconsidering the mission date, location, or communications architecture.

This demonstrates the importance of evaluating multiple environmental factors rather than relying on a single indicator when planning a lunar mission.

Benefits and Intended Impact

ORVYNTEX aims to bridge the gap between complex scientific information and practical, interactive mission planning.

Its primary benefits include:

Scientific accessibility: Transforming astronomical calculations into intuitive visualizations that can be understood by students, educators, researchers, and space enthusiasts.

Informed mission planning: Helping users understand how landing location and mission timing influence solar illumination, communication opportunities, and operational conditions.

Integrated learning: Connecting astronomy, engineering, robotics, resource management, and human physiology within a unified experience.

Safe experimentation: Allowing users to explore different scenarios and operational decisions without the cost, complexity, or risks associated with real-world lunar missions.

Educational engagement: Encouraging curiosity about space exploration through interactive simulations, visual explanations, and knowledge challenges.

Our intended impact is to inspire future scientists, engineers, and explorers while demonstrating the importance of data-driven decisions in sustainable lunar exploration.

We also aim to highlight how technologies and operational practices developed in northern Chile can contribute conceptually to future space exploration systems.

Scientific Methods and Development Tools

The scientific foundation of ORVYNTEX uses astronomical position calculations based on Jean Meeus' Astronomical Algorithms, including methods for calculating solar and lunar positions.

Lunar orientation calculations are based on the IAU/WGCCRE 2009 rotational model, and astronomical results were compared against NASA's JPL Horizons system.

The project also incorporates publicly available lunar geographic information and references resources such as:

  • NASA JPL Horizons.
  • Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC) QuickMap.
  • NASA Moon Trek.
  • Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) elevation data as a reference for future terrain-based improvements.

The platform integrates an interactive web interface, astronomical computation, dynamic data visualization, three-dimensional educational simulation, and mission reporting.

The current astronomical model uses a spherical lunar horizon with an adjustable horizon mask. A future development stage will incorporate terrain-based horizon profiles derived from LOLA elevation data to account more accurately for the effects of mountains, crater walls, and local topography on illumination and Earth visibility.

Factors Considered During Development

Our team considered several interconnected scientific, technological, and human factors throughout the development of the project:

Solar energy availability: Understanding how illumination conditions influence potential energy generation and the continuity of lunar operations.

Communication: Evaluating the geometric visibility of Earth and recognizing the potential need for relay satellites when direct communication is unavailable.

Landing location and timing: Recognizing that the suitability of a lunar site changes depending on its geographic position and the selected mission period.

Lunar terrain: Considering the importance of local topography, crater geometry, elevation, and terrain-related obstructions.

Human survival: Exploring the effects of reduced gravity, environmental constraints, resource availability, and the physiological challenges of living beyond Earth.

Autonomous operations: Investigating how remote control, robotic exploration, and centralized decision-making could support future lunar activities.

Scientific accuracy and transparency: Comparing astronomical calculations against an established reference system, documenting our methodology, and clearly communicating the limitations of the current prototype.

Accessibility and user experience: Designing a bilingual, interactive platform that makes complex scientific concepts approachable for users with different levels of technical knowledge.

Sustainability and future development: Considering how long-term lunar operations could benefit from renewable energy, local resources, autonomous systems, and carefully planned infrastructure.
